findings.short: Engineers worry that AI incident tools will deskill or replace them, and about what those tools can touch in production. On the pages checked, none of the {vendors_rated} options shows proof on either.
findings.headline: Deskilling or replacement ({count:deskills_or_replaces_engineers} of {n_base} posts) and production access ({count:data_access_and_security}): on the pages checked, every option asserts and none shows proof. Investigations is closest on access.
findings.note: Read one by one, {read:deskills_or_replaces_engineers:fit_all} of the {count:deskills_or_replaces_engineers} deskilling posts and {read:data_access_and_security:fit_all} of the {count:data_access_and_security} access posts fit their label; the rest are general complaints about AI.
findings.implication: Closest to proof on deskilling is Datadog: named customers say newer engineers get a head start, but nobody shows anyone learning. On access, Investigations makes one of the two strictest promises (its only change is a pull request you review) and is the only option to name an outside audit, SOC 2; PagerDuty's and Resolve's agents can act on their own within rules you set. Showing how “pull request only” is enforced, and linking the SOC 2 report, would turn that into proof.
findings.why: Round 2 review (20 Oct), simulated: no ranking words (23 vs 20 is within label noise); counts given with a full read of both rows; credits incident.io's access promise and SOC 2; names Datadog as the nearest to proof on deskilling (engineer, competitive PMM and marketing-lead reviews).

findings.headline: {diy:uses} of {n_base} posts use or recommend a general AI tool for incident work, {diy:uses:positive} of them positive about it; only {diy:uses:unneeded} of those {diy:uses} argue that makes a dedicated product unnecessary.
findings.implication: incident.io argues on its blog that in-house builds rarely measure accuracy, and ships a plugin for the agents engineers already use. The missing piece is a published score: Investigations against a bare model on the same past incidents, which its daily backtests could produce without showing any customer's data.
findings.why: Round 2 review (20 Oct), simulated: the 13 'product unnecessary' included 5 posts outside the 73 users; the subset is now computed (diy:uses:unneeded). Backtests can give a score without publishing customer incidents.

findings.headline: {either:wrong_or_hallucinated_cause+cant_verify_reasoning} of {n_base} posts say the AI gets the cause wrong or that its reasoning can't be checked.
findings.implication: Investigations shows proof on both: a measured jump in accurate early updates, and an incident write-up in which its conclusion was checked against the code. The next question is how often it's wrong. Each customer can see its own rate on the Investigations homepage, and incident.io's buyer's guide tells evaluators to ask vendors for precision and recall; a published figure from its backtests would be the first from any option here.
findings.why: Round 2 review (20 Oct), simulated: 'every hypothesis linked to its sources' is a feature claim, not proof; the cant-verify rating rests on the incident write-up.
